units.text: Start on the left. The corporate client asks its DNS server for the private application name. The conditional forwarder sends matching queries toward the inbound endpoint addresses.
Follow the query across the private connection into the endpoint VPC. The two endpoint interfaces provide addresses in different Availability Zones; configure the corporate forwarder to use both.
Move to the right. Resolver answers using the private hosted zone associated with the endpoint VPC. The response goes back to the corporate DNS server and then the client.
With the full diagram visible, check private connectivity and both TCP and UDP port fifty-three. Remote forwarders target inbound endpoint addresses, not the VPC base plus two resolver address.
Begin with the AWS workload and VPC Resolver on the left. A query for the corporate namespace matches a forwarding rule associated with the client's VPC.
Read the rule box above the arrow. It specifies the domain suffix, outbound endpoint and target DNS addresses. The most specific matching suffix selects the forwarding rule.
Follow the arrow through the outbound endpoint to corporate DNS. Routes and endpoint security must permit the query and its response across the connection to the target servers.
Return to the full slide. Outbound describes the query direction from AWS. Check reverse lookup rules separately, and verify the complete DNS path before testing the application connection.
Trace the upper row. Corporate DNS forwards the AWS private namespace to an inbound endpoint. The private hosted zone is the authority for that namespace in this design.
Now trace the lower row. An AWS client uses an associated forwarding rule and outbound endpoint to reach the corporate authority for the corporate namespace.

Inspect the warnings at the bottom. Forwarding the same suffix back and forth creates a loop. Namespace delegation follows an authority chain and requires the appropriate endpoint and rule configuration.
With both directions visible, explain who owns each suffix before choosing a rule. Validate the query and response paths, and avoid broad forwarding that unexpectedly captures your private names.

Compare the two upper panels. The inbound endpoint receives queries from corporate forwarders; the outbound endpoint sends queries to corporate DNS targets. Each design spreads endpoint addresses across Availability Zones.
Read the security cards below. For the port fifty-three design shown, inbound rules allow approved forwarders, and outbound rules allow the target DNS servers. Security groups track return traffic.

Move to the network and resilience cards. Stateless network ACLs need query and response paths, including ephemeral ports. Provide routing, multiple endpoint addresses and target servers, and monitor capacity.
Review the whole slide. These security group controls apply to endpoint network interfaces. Test both TCP and UDP DNS, and distinguish endpoint access from the Amazon-provided VPC resolver.
